newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus - Bundesbank denies Tietmeyer wants EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Bundesbank denies Tietmeyer wants EMU delay.

text.p: The German central bank on Sunday dismissed a report that it was concerned about whether European monetary union (EMU) could go ahead on time and wanted to make sure any postponement was orderly.

For the second time this month, the news weekly Der Spiegel said Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer had expressed his concerns about the timing of EMU to top politicians including Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

It also said Tietmeyer had told bankers he believed a plan should be devised to ensure that any postponement of a European Union single currency beyond the planned January 1, 1999 start date would be orderly.
The Bundesbank dismissed the report out of hand.
"Mr Tietmeyer has not in any of his talks urged a delay of monetary union or a plan for a delay," Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber told Reuters.
The Bundesbank chief has never publicly called for an EMU delay and firmly denied a separate Der Spiegel report earlier this month which said he had suggested a postponement.
Tietmeyer then said he was committed to the Maastricht treaty, which sets down the timetable for currency union.
The latest edition of Der Spiegel said Tietmeyer was worried that potential EMU participants were not showing enough commitment to fiscal discipline.

But separately, Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp told a meeting of the opposition Social Democrats on Saturday it was crucial that the euro should start on time in order to prevent potential disturbance on financial markets.

Talk of Bundesbank concern about EMU has been fuelled by a last month's rift with the government, when Tietmeyer shot down Waigel's plans to use profits generated from revaluing Bundesbank gold and currency reserves for the 1997 budget.
Germany is struggling desperately to meet the Maastricht treaty budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997.
But the staunchly independent central bank said the revaluation plan impeded its operations and threatened Germany's image as a hardliner on monetary union.
Tietmeyer has declared himself willing only to accept a modified version of the plan, and ruled out any impact on 1997 accounts from the procedure.
Talks are continuing and Waigel said on Saturday he planned to meet Tietmeyer to discuss the issue this week.

"We have a solution in sight which we will achieve in agreement with the Bundesbank," Waigel said at a meeting in Bavaria of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Any fight between politicians and the Bundesbank does us no good," Waigel added.
The revised revaluation proposal is expected to focus on currency reserves, while the issue of revaluing gold may have been put on the back burner.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at around 13.7 billion marks compared with a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
